newsitem.title: UK: Asian transport fuel demand to rise 8 pct a year.
newsitem.headline: Asian transport fuel demand to rise 8 pct a year.

text.p: Sharp growth in demand for tranport fuels in the Asia-Pacific region will continue well into the next century but will slow down from recent gains of nearly nine percent a year, analysts Wood Mackenzie said.

Between 1995 and 2000 consumption is forecast to rise by eight percent per year, slowing to five percent each year in the period 2000 to 2005 and then to 3.5 percent between 2005 and 2010, Wood Mackenzie said in a report published on Wednesday.

Transport fuels are a key factor behind "extraordinary growth" in oil demand which, driven by the Asian "tiger" economies, has seen demand rise to 800 million tonnes in 1995 from 600 million in 1990, the report said.
Transport fuel demand is likely to become even more important as China and India develop their economies.
China, India and Indonesia, Asia's most populous nations, have low but quickly rising per capita energy use.
Chinese gasoline demand grew by 13 percent a year from 1990 to 1995 and in India demand for transportation gas oil rose eight percent a year over the same period.
Unchecked demand growth in transport fuels could be maintained into the long term but the existing refining infrastructure will find it difficult to cope with demand, the report said.
Political and bureaucratic barriers to refining investment are likely to remain, so imports of finished products are likely to rise.
Governments faced with mounting import bills will look to limit demand growth, for example through environmental measures to improve fuel quality.
Fiscal reforms will move subsidised energy markets towards world markets, resulting in higher prices for consumers.
Other restraining factors include the slowdown of expansion in already inadequate road systems and moves to more efficient cars.
Oil demand in the region will continue to expand at a faster rate than anywhere else in the world, the report said. --London newsroom +44 171 542 4948
